title: Parenting Is Slow Work
author: The Daily Dad
summary: A short Daily Dad reflection on the disheartening sense that children aren't listening or absorbing what we tell them, anchored to a letter from Mary Shelley's father about the slow, invisible work of parenting. The seeds an attentive father sows often appear to fall on ungrateful soil, but the writer of the letter looks back to find that the happiest operations were proceeding quietly and unobserved, unfolding at the moment they were most needed. The piece asks parents to be patient with the surface appearance of indifference and to keep sowing, toiling, and tilling because the formation is happening beneath the visible. The closing posture is encouragement rather than data: even when a child seems to ignore everything you say, formation may be in process. The reflection draws moral seriousness from a 19th-century literary parent rather than from contemporary psychology, situating fatherhood as the patient long-haul work it has always been.
points: Parental words can feel wasted in the moment because children's apparent indifference hides the slow underground work of formation, which only shows itself later.
Mary Shelley's father wrote that the seeds he sowed seemed to fall on ungrateful soil, but the happiest operations were proceeding quietly until they unfolded at the moment of greatest importance.
The right parental posture in the face of unresponsiveness is patience, not louder volume; the work is slow because formation is slow, and the visible surface is not the operative layer.
Keeping at it (sowing, toiling, tilling) is itself the strategy; consistency over time is what gives the seeds their chance to take root.
Treating fatherhood as long-haul work shifts the success metric from immediate response to eventual character, which is the harder but more honest measure.
quotes: Why won't they listen? Why do they do the opposite of what you ask of them? Are you just wasting your breath? Parenting can be disheartening like that. You talk, you explain, you repeat yourself, and it seems like nothing is getting through those thick little skulls.
Seeds of intellect and knowledge, seeds of moral judgment and conduct, I have sown; but the soil for a long while seemed ungrateful to the tiller's care.
It was not so; the happiest operations were going on quietly and unobserved, and at the moment when it was of the most importance, they unfolded themselves to the delight of every beholder.
We think they're not listening, they're not observing, that they don't appreciate the lessons we're trying to impart. And maybe they don't. Not yet.

But under the surface, something is happening. The seeds are taking root. Our job is to be patient. No matter how impossible it seems, we have to keep sowing and toiling and tilling.” Archived from The Daily Dad on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
